extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, and indexers preparing manuscripts using the Chicago Manual of Style (author-date system) for books, articles, and e-publications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing author-date (Chicago) citations across special cases (reprints, multivolume works, websites, social media, manuscripts, audiovisuals, legal documents, patents, etc.) and for preparing/editing back-of-book and embedded indexes. Includes formatting rules, examples, and recommended practices for indexers and publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short title forms for in-text author-date references
rubrics_metrics.description: In the text, a short version of the title (up to four words) may be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike short forms for titles in notes and bibliography style, short forms for in-text references must include the first word of the title (aside from any article) to facilitate alphabetical lookup. See examples (15.34, 15.34 referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reprint and modern edition dating in author-date references
rubrics_metrics.description: When citing a reprint or modern edition, it is sometimes desirable to include the original date of publication. Whether or not original-publication information is included, the original date is listed first, in parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the pagination of the original edition does not match that of the reprint, indicate the edition cited. In-text parentheses are rendered as square brackets: (Austen [1813] 2003). Examples: Austen, Jane. (1813) 2003. Pride and Prejudice. Reprint, New York: Penguin Classics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering multiple works by the same author
rubrics_metrics.description: For more than one work by the same author, the first date determines placement in the reference list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show original-date-first ordering when original dates are given: Maitland (1898) 1998 precedes ——. (1909) 1926. If original date is not prioritized, modern-source date can be used (see guidance on when to privilege original vs modern date).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of modern-source date when original date is unimportant
rubrics_metrics.description: When the original date is less important to the discussion, use the date of the modern source. The original date may be included at the end of the reference list entry but need not be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Trollope, Anthony. 1977. The Claverings. First published 1866–67. Text citations use (Trollope 1977).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multivolume works and date ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: When a multivolume, multiyear work is included as an entry, the range of dates for the work as a whole follows the author’s name; text citations should include a volume number with references to specific page numbers or to cite a specific volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an individual volume is listed, the date for that volume follows the author's name; information about the work as a whole follows information about the individual volume. If the work is not yet completed, the date of the first volume is followed by an en dash (no space). Text citations of volumes listed individually do not include the volume number even with page references. Examples: Tillich, Paul. 1951–63. Systematic Theology. (Tillich 1951–63, 1:133) ; Hayek, F. A. 2011. The Constitution of Liberty: ... Vol. 17 ... (Hayek 2011, 329).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-references for contributions in edited multiauthor volumes
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual contributions to an edited volume may include cross-references to an entry for the volume as a whole to avoid repeating information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cross-references only if more than a few individual contributions to the same volume are cited or if the volume itself is also cited in the text; otherwise include full publication details in each contribution's entry. Example forms: Draper, Joan E. 1987. “Paris by the Lake: Sources of Burnham’s Plan of Chicago.” In Zukowsky 1987, 107–19.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-date citations for letters in published collections
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters in published collections should be cited by the date of the collection; dates of individual correspondence should be woven into the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example reference-list entries: Adams, Henry. 1930. Letters of Henry Adams, 1858–1891. In-text: In a letter to Charles Milnes Gaskell from London, March 30, 1868 (Adams 1930, 141).

rubrics_metrics.name: No date (n.d.) usage
rubrics_metrics.description: When the publication date cannot be ascertained, the abbreviation n.d. takes the place of the year in the reference list entry and text citations. n.d. remains lowercase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A guessed date may be substituted in brackets with a question mark to indicate uncertainty (e.g., [1750?]). For website content cited by access date, use n.d. and include access date. Examples: (Nano [1750?]) (Nano, n.d.). See also guidance at 15.50 and 15.54.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forthcoming designation
rubrics_metrics.description: Forthcoming can stand in place of the date for books under contract with a publisher and already titled but for which a publication date is not yet known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve 'forthcoming' for works under contract; if page numbers are available include them. Books not under contract are treated as unpublished manuscripts. In text citations, forthcoming is preceded by a comma: (Faraday, forthcoming).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviating periodical titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Many scientific publications prefer abbreviated journal titles; ISO 4 is the main authority for abbreviating words in serial titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard abbreviation lists include BIOSIS Serial Sources and the NLM Catalog; consult Scientific Style and Format or AMA Manual of Style for detailed lists. Examples and bibliographic references provided (bibliog. 4.7, 4.5, 1.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting issue numbers (parentheses vs commas)
rubrics_metrics.description: When only a volume and issue number are available, the issue number is placed in parentheses. When only an issue number is used (no volume), the issue number is set off by commas and not enclosed in parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare examples: Glass and Levchak. 2014. American Journal of Sociology 119 (4): 1002–46. Meyerovitch. 1959. Diogenes, no. 25, 84–117.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon after volume number when no issue number
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is no issue number and no month/season, the page reference follows the volume number separated by a colon with no intervening space. If month/season is included, it is enclosed in parentheses and a space follows the colon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Gunderson and Leal. 2015. American Naturalist 185:653–64. If month included: American Naturalist 185 (May): 653–64.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing newspapers and magazines
rubrics_metrics.description: It is usually sufficient to cite newspaper and magazine articles entirely within the text; if a reference-list entry is needed, repeat the year with month and day to avoid confusion. If an article is unsigned, the newspaper title stands in place of the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Kauffman, Stanley. 1989. Review... New Republic, October 9, 1989, 24–25. Meikle example with URL included. Unsigned example: New York Times. 2002. “In Texas...” July 30, 2002. (New York Times 2002). See 15.34, 15.37 for related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Websites: when to include access dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Chicago requires an access date for website citations only if no date of publication or revision can be determined from the source; in such cases record n.d. as the date in the reference list and in-text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Alliance for Linguistic Diversity. n.d. “Balkan Romani.” Endangered Languages. Accessed April 6, 2016. URL. If a date of publication/revision exists, use that year and repeat year with month and day in the reference list to avoid confusion (e.g., Google. 2016. “Privacy Policy.” Last modified March 25, 2016.). See 14.12 and 15.37.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing blogs
rubrics_metrics.description: Blogs and blog posts are cited by adapting recommendations for newspaper/magazine articles; often it is sufficient to cite blog posts in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reference-list entry is needed, repeat year with month and day. Comments are not included in reference lists and should be cited in the text as comments on the related post; references to an entire blog are made in the text with URL in parentheses. Examples: Germano, William. 2014/2017 post example; comment citation example provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing social media
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media content can be cited in author-date format by adapting recommendations; often text-only citation is sufficient, but frequently cited accounts or extensive threads may be included in a reference list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the reference list include real name and screen name if both available; in text cite the name under which the entry is listed. Repeat year with month and day in the reference list. Comments are cited only in the text; direct or private messages shared and received by the author are cited as personal communications. Examples: Chicago Manual of Style Facebook post; Diaz 2016; O’Brien tweet example; Souza Instagram example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpublished interviews and personal communications
rubrics_metrics.description: In parenthetical citations, use terms like personal communication (pers. comm.) or unpublished data after the person’s name. Reference-list entries are unneeded, but each person cited must be fully identified elsewhere in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If medium matters and is not mentioned in text, include it in the parenthetical reference (e.g., Jonathan Lee, Facebook direct message to author, May 5, 2017). Add a date in parentheses after the name unless mentioned in text. Avoid et al. in such citations. Examples: (Julie Cantor, pers. comm.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript collections (author-date format)
rubrics_metrics.description: When citing manuscript collections, it is unnecessary to use n.d. Dates of individual items should be mentioned in the text when applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only one item from a collection is mentioned, the entry may begin with the writer’s name (if known) and n.d. may be appropriate. Examples: Egmont Manuscripts. Phillipps Collection. University of Georgia Library; Kallen, Horace. Papers. YIVO Institute. In-text example: Oglethorpe wrote to the trustees on January 13, 1733 (Egmont Manuscripts). See also 15.44.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents and standards with multiple dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite patents and other documents that include more than one date by listing the year of issue repeated to avoid ambiguity and by giving filing and issue dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Tizuka, Masanori, and Hideki Tanaka. 1986. Cement admixture. US Patent 4,586,960, filed June 26, 1984, and issued May 6, 1986. For examples of standards cited in author-date format see 15.37.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quoting from secondary sources ('quoted in') discouraged
rubrics_metrics.description: Citing a source from a secondary source is generally discouraged because authors should examine works they cite; if the original is unavailable, mention the original author and date in the text and cite the secondary source in the reference list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ‘In Louis Zukofsky’s “Sincerity and Objectification,” from the February 1931 issue of Poetry magazine (quoted in Costello 1981)...’ Use secondary citation only when original cannot be accessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audiovisual recordings and multimedia citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiovisual recordings and other multimedia can be cited in author-date format by adapting the guidelines for recorded media; often it is appropriate to list such materials in running text or group them in a separate discography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite the format consulted but give information about the original source if available; privilege the date of the original recording. Whom to list as 'author' depends on citation focus. Examples: Coolidge [1920?] speech on Library of Congress site; Grande and Augustyn 2011 iPad ed.; Holiday 1958 track example; Lyiscott TED video example. Live performances generally are not cited in a reference list—incorporate details into the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live performances
rubrics_metrics.description: Live performances, which cannot be consulted as such by readers, are generally not cited in a reference list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate details about the performance into the text. Example: 'In a performance of Lin-Manuel Miranda’s Hamilton at the Richard Rodgers Theatre in New York on February 2, 2016, ...'

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and public documents: prefer notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal publications use notes for documentation and few include bibliographies; works using author-date that need more than occasional legal/public-document citations should use supplementary footnotes or endnotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This advice does not extend to documents collected in secondary sources or published as freestanding works, which can be adapted to author-date. For full discussion and examples see 14.269–305. In legal style, parentheses within parentheses are used, and Chicago advises using notes for legal/public documents to avoid awkward text constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and value of a human-created index
rubrics_metrics.description: A good (back-of-the-book) index gathers substantive terms and subjects, sorts them alphabetically, provides cross-references and specific locators or links, and makes a longer work more accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even for searchable texts, an index provides insurance against fruitless queries and unintended results and can do what plain search cannot. The chapter models back-of-book indexes but notes applicability to electronic formats that lack fixed page numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who should compile the index
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal indexer sees the work as a whole, understands emphasis and relationships across parts, anticipates reader lookups, and is scrupulous, analytical, widely read, familiar with publishing practices, and deadline-capable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors sometimes make good indexers but not always; many authors should enlist a professional indexer, who can better meet publisher requirements and reflect on choices under deadline constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing schedule and deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Most book indexes are prepared between issuance of page proofs and their return to the typesetter—usually about four weeks. Volume indexes for journals may allow several months but the final issue may give only a week for finishing the index.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indexing requires reflection and stopping to evaluate choices; professional indexers are often better equipped to manage this under tight schedules. See also publishing-process timing (2.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and limits of software in indexing
rubrics_metrics.description: Concordances and automated lists of terms can be produced automatically, but a concordance is not the same as an index; most indexes are produced from scratch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Word processors help with entering and sorting entries and managing cross-references; dedicated indexing software can automate formatting and cross-referencing and is a good investment for professionals. See 16.104 and related notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single versus multiple indexes
rubrics_metrics.description: A single, comprehensive index (concepts, names, other subjects) is recommended for most works, but certain publications may include separate indexes (e.g., index of named authors, author-and-title index, first-lines index).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple indexes appear, make them visually distinct and use separate running heads indicating each index's title (e.g., Index of Names, Index of Subjects). Example differences for a biological work: names in roman type with capitals and no subentries; subject index headings begin lowercase with many subentries; taxonomic index headings in italics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedded indexes for electronic publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Embedded indexes consist of key terms anchored with codes to particular points in an electronic text to facilitate targeted searches—similar selection principles as traditional back-of-book indexes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embedded indexes increase precision in search results (example of 'because' leading to Beatles song 'Because' rather than conjunction occurrences). Many journal publishers use standard keyword vocabularies instead of traditional indexes. Anchoring back-of-book index entries to electronic files facilitates hyperlinked e-book indexes (see 16.13). EPUB specifications exist for e-book indexes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main headings: form and capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: The main heading is normally a noun or noun phrase (name of a person, place, object, or abstraction); an adjective alone should almost never be a heading—pair with a noun or invert to put the keyword first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headings are typically followed by locators and sometimes cross-references. Capitalization rules: first word of a main heading normally capitalized only if capitalized in text (proper noun, genus name, title). Traditional full capitalization of main headings is recommended only when subentries are very numerous; sciences usually avoid initial capitals. See 16.11 for capitalization specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Index subentries: when and how to break entries
rubrics_metrics.description: An entry that requires more than five or six locators is usually broken into subentries to spare readers unnecessary excursions; subentries include a heading, page references, and rarely cross-references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subheadings often form a grammatical relationship with the main heading (heading + subheading = phrase) or form divisions/units within the larger category. Use sub-subentries where necessary. See examples: 'capitalism: and American Sovietism, 273, 274; bourgeoisie as symbol of, 4, 13;' and 'Native American peoples: Ahualucos, Chichimecs ...'. See 16.27 and 16.28 for sub-subentry rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial lowercase letters in main headings and subheadings
rubrics_metrics.description: The first word of a main heading is normally capitalized only if capitalized in text; subheadings are always lowercased unless the keyword is capitalized in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditional all-capitalized main headings are recommended only when many subentries make navigation easier. In scientific indexes, avoid initial capitals because textual distinctions may be crucial. Examples demonstrate when 'Khrushchev' versus other subentries are capitalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locators in indexes: page/paragraph/section numbers and range rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Locators are usually page numbers but can be paragraph numbers, section numbers, etc. When discussion continues more than a page/paragraph/section, give the first and last numbers (inclusive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use abbreviations ff or et seq.; scattered references should be indicated by separate locators (e.g., 34, 35, 36). Avoid 'passim'—prefer individual locators. Use en dash for ranges; see inclusive-number rules (16.14–16.16) for formatting specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linked indexes for e-books and reflowable formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Indexes for e-book formats should at minimum be linked to the text; for reflowable text, link index entries directly to the passage rather than relying on page numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page-number data from the printed format can be the basis for links, but for reflowable formats the actual location may shift; linking directly to passages (or numbered paragraphs in a manual) yields better reader experience. Requires publisher/indexer intervention. See EPUB specs from the International Digital Publishing Forum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusive-number formatting system
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers vary in preferences for inclusive (continuing) numbers; Chicago prefers a traditional efficient system for abbreviating the second number depending on magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules summarized: less than 100—use all digits (3–10; 71–72); 101–109 use changed part only (101–8); 110–199 use two digits unless more are needed (321–28); 100 or multiples use all digits (100–104); Roman numerals always given in full (xxv–xxviii). Follow the same form in text and index.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-references: see vs see also and usage principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-references are of two main kinds—see references and see also references—and are treated differently depending on whether they refer to a main heading or a subheading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set 'see' and 'see also' in italics (unless exceptions apply). Use cross-references with discretion—overuse may irritate readers and signal need for consolidation. Avoid 'blind cross-references' (see leading only to another see). If the entry to which a see refers is about the same length as the see reference, double posting (listing page numbers under both headings) is often more useful. Electronic cross-references should link to the referred terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'See' references following a main heading: punctuation and order
rubrics_metrics.description: When a see reference follows a main heading it is preceded by a period and 'See' is capitalized; if two or more see references are needed, arrange them alphabetically and separate with semicolons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See references reflect capitalization and word order of the main heading. Examples: 'adolescence. See teenagers; youth' ; 'American Communist Party. See Communist Party (American)'. See also guidance on not creating chains of see references.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'See' references following a subheading: parenthetical usage
rubrics_metrics.description: When a see reference follows a subheading, it is put in parentheses and 'see' is lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to run-in and indented indexes and to sub-subentries. Example: 'statistical material, 16, 17, 89; as on-line supplement (see supplements, online); proofreading, 183'. See 16.27 and 16.28 for related subentry rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'See under' references to subheadings
rubrics_metrics.description: When a cross-reference directs readers to a subentry under another main heading, 'see under' may be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'see under' to point to specific subentries rather than to main headings only. No example in the excerpt beyond the guidance that 'see under' is appropriate for directing to a subheading.
